solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

parts.note: a 'minuteman' read as a minute, tiny man needs a vehicle of matching smallness: a mini taxi

explanation.surface: A question about how an American militiaman of the Revolution got about.
explanation.walkthrough: A minuteman was a colonial American militiaman ready at a minute's notice; here 'minute' is read as tiny. A minicab is a British taxi booked by phone rather than hailed.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hired car is a form of transport, and its name fits a very small passenger.

indicators.note: an unorthodox arrangement of these letters is a rearranged one

explanation.surface: A doctor admitting to unconventional ways in a secret code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unorthodox' shuffles CODE and IM.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal word is a colloquial term for a physician.

clue.text: Luce not going out to bat

indicators.note: the letters go out of their order and form a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A woman named Luce declines to go out to bat in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going out' rearranges LUCE NOT; 'bat' looks like cricket but is the flying mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: This large brown species is a European bat.

parts.note: Sing Sing suggests the New York prison and a disreputable woman inmate, but read as singing it means a woman with a low voice in a choir

explanation.surface: A disreputable woman locked up in Sing Sing prison.
explanation.walkthrough: Sing Sing is a notorious New York prison, so 'low lady' looks like a criminal; it is the lowest female singing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest female voice part is sung by a woman with a deep register.

clue.text: D'Orsay doubtless knew the boon of her chic

parts.note: a boon is a blessing, something welcome
'ton' is fashionable style, high society's chic

explanation.surface: Count D'Orsay surely appreciated the gift of a lady's elegance.
explanation.walkthrough: Count D'Orsay, the Regency dandy, lived for years with Marguerite, Countess of Blessington, the literary hostess.
explanation.definitionFit: The Countess of this title was the companion and hostess of the dandy Count D'Orsay.

clue.text: To beg the unjust steward was

definitions.text: To beg the unjust steward was

parts.words: To beg the unjust steward was
parts.note: completes the steward's words in the parable of the unjust steward in Luke's gospel: 'to beg I am ...'

explanation.surface: A remark about the dishonest manager in Jesus's parable and his reluctance to beg.
explanation.walkthrough: In Luke 16:3 the steward says 'I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed'; the clue asks what he was about begging.
explanation.definitionFit: The parable's steward says begging would bring him shame, so this is how he felt about it.

parts.note: a jack is a male donkey, and a laughing jackass is the kookaburra

explanation.surface: Someone called Jack in a fit of giggles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name; a jack is a male donkey, and the kookaburra is the 'laughing jackass', so the animal in that name is the one wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: A male donkey is called a jack, and the word completes the laughing jackass.

clue.text: He has a bit more than he can digest

definitions.text: He has a bit more than he can digest

parts.words: He has a bit more than he can digest
parts.note: 'bit' read as the metal mouthpiece of a bridle, not a morsel

explanation.surface: Someone who has bitten off more than he can chew.
explanation.walkthrough: The bit is the bar in a riding animal's mouth, which it holds but never swallows.
explanation.definitionFit: This riding animal carries a bridle's metal bit in its mouth that it cannot eat.

indicators.note: clipping a word cuts off its tail, the final letter

parts.note: Shakespeare's Romeo belongs to the family named Montague

explanation.surface: A lady trimming the hair of a boyfriend named Romeo.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu was an 18th-century writer and traveller; 'clipped' drops the final E from Romeo's family name.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, the letter-writer, is known by this surname.

parts.note: 'hinges on' read as literally hinged rather than dependent: paintings on two hinged panels

explanation.surface: A claim that art depends on certain things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hinges on' sounds like 'depends on', but these are pictures painted on two panels joined by a hinge, often altarpieces.
explanation.definitionFit: These paired, hinged painted panels are works of art built around a hinge.

clue.text: They have a glassy look, well wined

definitions.text: They have a glassy look, well wined

parts.words: They have a glassy look, well wined
parts.note: sounds like drunks with glazed eyes, but describes glass vessels that hold plenty of wine

explanation.surface: A picture of heavy drinkers staring glassily after too much wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glassy look' and 'well wined' suggest tipsy people; the subject is the glass bottles wine is poured into for serving.
explanation.definitionFit: These stoppered glass vessels are made of glass and are filled with wine before serving.

parts.note: Sisyphus endlessly pushed his boulder uphill, and Dorcas, the biblical seamstress, sewed garments: one phrase covers dashing uphill and sewing something quickly

explanation.surface: A request to hurry along two figures, one from Greek myth and one from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: Sisyphus would speed by dashing up his hill; Dorcas (Acts 9), who made clothes for the poor, would speed by quickly sewing a garment together, which is also to run one up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both to climb at a dash and to sew something hastily, matching each figure.

parts.note: a 'jar' is a harsh grating noise, so this is the jarring call the nightjar makes

explanation.surface: A play on the word jar inside the bird's own name.
explanation.walkthrough: The nightjar is named for its jarring, whirring night call; the clue asks for the word for that sound.
explanation.definitionFit: This word names the low trilling whirr of the nightjar, a harsh noise of the kind called a jar.

clue.text: Office assistant concerned with hush-hush new ray

parts.note: something hush-hush is kept confidential

indicators.note: a new version of the word ray is a rearrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: An office worker linked to some classified new kind of ray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concerned with' is only a link; the anagram signal is 'new', acting on the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An office clerk who handles correspondence and diaries is a standard office helper.

parts.note: a length of about 100 fathoms is a cable, and something made by knitting needles is a stitch; the Needles suggests the rocks off the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: A depth sounding near the Needles, the rocks off the Isle of Wight.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are chalk stacks off the Isle of Wight, so the clue looks nautical; a cable is a nautical length of about 100 fathoms, and needles make stitches in knitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitting pattern of twisted ropes is made with needles and named after a ship's rope.

parts.note: Old Nosey was the Duke of Wellington's nickname; a Northamptonshire town's name looks like a version of 'Wellington's borough'

explanation.surface: A query about a nickname for someone known as Nosey in Northamptonshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The Duke of Wellington was nicknamed 'Old Nosey' for his large nose. Northants is Northamptonshire, an English county containing a market town whose name reads as his borough.
explanation.definitionFit: This market town in Northamptonshire has a name that resembles the Iron Duke's title plus 'borough'.

parts.note: 'see red' read literally rather than as getting angry: the red lamp on the back of a vehicle

explanation.surface: Something that makes drivers trying to pass furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See red' sounds like anger; the drivers behind simply see the red lamp at the back of the car ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: The red lamp at the back of a vehicle is what following drivers see.

clue.text: Flood waters finally did so (AV spelling); 5 dn carried on

definitions.text: Flood waters finally did so (AV spelling)

parts.note: the answer to 5 down, a donkey
to wage war is to carry it on

explanation.surface: A biblical comment on the Flood, with a donkey carrying on.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 8:1 in the Authorised Version (AV, the King James Bible) says 'the waters asswaged', the old spelling of 'assuaged'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the floodwaters subsided, which the King James Bible spells with a double S.

clue.text: The best is not from the briny

definitions.text: The best is not from the briny

parts.words: The best is not from the briny
parts.note: the finest people are called a seasoning from the land, and that seasoning comes from soil rather than the sea

explanation.surface: A claim that the finest things do not come out of the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The briny' is the sea, where most salt is taken from; the phrase from Matthew 5:13 names salt from the land instead, and means the finest, most worthy people.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from the Sermon on the Mount, describes thoroughly good, dependable people, the best there are.

parts.note: the offspring of the zodiac's lion, Leo: the meteor shower that seems to radiate from that constellation

explanation.surface: Lion cubs born under a sign of the zodiac.
explanation.walkthrough: Leo is the Lion of the zodiac; the November meteor shower named after it reads like the Lion's young.
explanation.definitionFit: These meteors appear to come from Leo, so they are the zodiac lion's offspring.

parts.note: suggests a card table for the game of bridge, but it is a framework holding up a bridge and also a kind of table

explanation.surface: Asking what table would suit a game of bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' looks like the card game; a framework of beams can hold up a railway bridge, and a board on such frames is a table.
explanation.definitionFit: A braced framework of beams supports bridges and, topped with a board, forms a table.

clue.text: " With —— bubbles winking at the brim " (Keats)

definitions.text: With —— bubbles winking at the brim " (Keats)

parts.words: With —— bubbles winking at the brim " (Keats)
parts.note: the missing word from Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale', describing a glass of wine

explanation.surface: A line from Keats about sparkling wine with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' has 'With beaded bubbles winking at the brim', of a beaker of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bubbles clinging like tiny drops at a glass's rim are described as forming little pearls.

parts.note: Doctor Who is the time-travelling hero of the BBC science-fiction series
'dunnit' is a colloquial spelling of 'done it', as in 'Who's done it?': the guilty party

explanation.surface: A space-travelling doctor is found guilty, and the police should book him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book him' sounds like a police order to charge a suspect; 'Book' is the definition, a detective novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A detective story is a kind of book in which the reader works out the culprit.

parts.note: the word that goes before 'marine' to make the blue pigment also means a political extremist

explanation.surface: Asking whether a certain marine soldier holds extreme views.
explanation.walkthrough: Put this word before 'marine' and you get the deep blue pigment ultramarine; on its own it means an extremist.
explanation.definitionFit: This word, used as a noun, names someone holding extreme political views.

clue.text: The rich man in his castle, the poor man at his gate

definitions.text: The rich man in his castle
definitions.meaning: a feudal lord, to whom allegiance is owed

definitions.text: the poor man at his gate
definitions.meaning: a vassal or subject who owes that allegiance

explanation.surface: A line from the hymn 'All Things Bright and Beautiful' about rich and poor.
explanation.walkthrough: The word applies both to a feudal superior and to the vassal bound to serve him, so it covers both men in the hymn line.
explanation.definitionFit: The feudal term names both the lord entitled to service and the subject who renders it.

clue.text: Can make a meal of this

definitions.text: Can make a meal of this

parts.words: Can make a meal of this
parts.note: 'meal' read as ground flour rather than a dinner: grain is milled into it

explanation.surface: A remark that something would make a decent dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meal' here is coarse ground grain, not lunch; this is corn brought to the mill to be ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Grain brought for milling is ground into meal, so it is what meal is made from.

clue.text: Motorway, it in turn being turnpiked, eased matters

parts.note: M1, read as MI, is Britain's first long motorway, London to Yorkshire

indicators.note: turning round means the word it is read backwards

parts.note: a turnpike road had gates where tolls were taken, so a turnpiked road is gated

explanation.surface: A motorway being made a toll road somehow calmed things down.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is written MI in crosswords; 'in turn' turns IT into TI.
explanation.definitionFit: To lessen severity or relieve a situation is to make things less harsh.

definitions.meaning: to spoil is to damage or ruin
the Scottish earldom named after a district of Aberdeenshire

explanation.surface: Ruining a noble's estate.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil is to ruin something, and the Earl of this title holds one of Scotland's oldest earldoms.

parts.note: 'hopelessly' read as being hopelessness itself: the giant of that name in Bunyan's 'Pilgrim's Progress'

explanation.surface: A sad description of someone hopelessly oversized.
explanation.walkthrough: Giant Despair imprisons Christian and Hopeful in Doubting Castle in Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress'; an outsize giant who embodies hopelessness.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunyan's giant is named for utter hopelessness, and as a giant he is enormous.

parts.note: a Vesta is a brand of match, whose tip burns when struck; the same term describes a rash person

explanation.surface: The Roman goddess of the hearth behaving in a strikingly rash way.
explanation.walkthrough: Vesta suggests the goddess, but it was a well-known brand of wax match; struck, its tip is burning, and the same compound means a rash, impetuous person.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash, quick-tempered person is described this way, as is a struck match tip.
